
--- PAGE 1 ---
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Movement Patterns of the Knee During Gait Following ACL
Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Mandeep Kaur1 • Daniel Cury Ribeiro1 • Jean-Claude Theis2 • Kate E. Webster3 •
Gisela Sole1
Published online: 2 March 2016
Ó Springer International Publishing Switzerland 2016
Abstract
Background Altered gait patterns following anterior
cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) may be associ-
ated with long-term impairments and post-traumatic
osteoarthritis.
Objective This systematic review and meta-analysis
compared lower limb kinematics and kinetics of the ACL
reconstructed knee with (1) the contralateral limb and (2)
healthy age-matched participants during walking, stair
climbing, and running. The secondary aim was to describe
the differences over time following ACLR for these
biomechanical variables.
Method Database searches were conducted from incep-
tion to July 2014 and updated in August 2015 for studies
exploring peak knee angles and moments following ACLR
during walking, stair negotiation, and running. Risk of bias
was assessed with a modified Downs and Black quality
index for all included studies, and meta-analyses were
performed. Forest plots were explored qualitatively for
recovery of gait variables over time after surgery.
Results A total of 40 studies were included in the review;
26 of these were rated as low risk and 14 as high risk of
bias. The meta-analysis included 27 studies. Strong to
moderate evidence indicated no significant difference in
peak flexion angles between ACLR and control groups
during walking and stair ascent. Strong evidence was found
for lower peak flexion moments in participants with ACLR
compared with control groups and contralateral limb dur-
ing walking and stair activities. Strong to moderate evi-
dence was found for lower peak adduction moment in
ACLR participants for the injured compared with the
contralateral limbs during walking and stair descent. The
qualitative assessment for recovery over time indicated a
pattern towards restoration of peak knee flexion angle with
increasing time from post-surgery. Peak knee adduction
moments were lower within the first year following surgery
and higher than controls during later phases (5 years).
Conclusion Joint kinematics are restored, on average,
6 years following reconstruction, while knee external
flexion moments remain lower than controls. Knee
adduction moments are lower during early phases follow-
ing reconstruction, but are higher than controls, on average,
5 years post-surgery. Findings indicate that knee function
is not fully restored following reconstruction, and long-
term maintenance programs may be needed.
Electronic supplementary material The online version of this
article (doi:10.1007/s40279-016-0510-4) contains supplementary
material, which is available to authorized users.

Key Points
This systematic review and meta-analysis compared
lower limb kinematics and kinetics of the anterior
cruciate ligament reconstructed (ACLR) knee with
(1) the contralateral limb and (2) healthy age-
matched participants during walking, stair climbing,
and running.
Knee kinematics are likely to be similar in ACLR
participants at 6 years following surgery compared
with healthy controls. Knee peak adduction moments
are lower in ACLR participants 3.5 years following
reconstruction compared with controls. After
4–5 years post-reconstruction, adduction moments
are higher than for uninjured controls. Peak knee
flexion moments are still lower after 5 years of
surgery in ACLR participants than in uninjured
controls.
The differences for knee moments indicate that the
knee function is not fully restored following
reconstruction, and long-term maintenance programs
may be needed.
1 Introduction
Ruptures of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) of the
knee are considered to be one of the most serious sport- and
exercise-related injuries in terms of the patients’ experi-
ences [1] and health costs [2]. The injury is most common
in sports such as netball, football, basketball, and handball,
and is often associated with non-contact mechanisms such
as jump landing and pivoting or twisting movements [3].
ACL injuries are treated surgically with reconstructions
plus rehabilitation or non-surgically with rehabilitation
alone [4]. The overall incidence of ACL reconstruction
(ACLR) has been reported as 23 % within 3 years of injury
[5]. A recent systematic review found that, following
ACLR, 81 % of patients return to some form of sport, but
only 55 % return to competitive sport [6]. In the long term,
50–70 % of patients with ACL rupture develop symptoms
associated with post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) after
10 years, adding further towards the personal and health
costs of these injuries [7]. Patients who undergo ACLR
appear to have a slightly higher risk of developing symp-
toms associated with knee osteoarthritis (OA) than those
managed non-surgically [8]. However, this evidence is
limited, and the prevalence of OA between individuals
treated with surgical reconstructions compared with non-
surgical management is still unclear [8–10].
Altered gait biomechanics, as indicated by joint angles
and moments, may indicate unresolved impairments fol-
lowing injury and surgery, and may also be a mechanical
contributing factor towards the development of PTOA [11,
12]. Differences for these biomechanical variables appear
to be important when comparing the injured side with the
contralateral uninjured side in patients with ACLR and also
with control groups. Individuals with ACLR have been
shown to walk with greater peak knee flexion angles than
controls in the early phases (\6 months), but with less
flexion (more extended) after 1 year post-surgery [13]. In
terms of joint loading in the frontal plane, external knee
adduction moments are often used as the measure of load
distribution in the frontal plane [14]. Increased peak
adduction moments during walking have been associated
with progression [12, 15] and severity of medial tibio-
femoral compartment OA [16]. Studies have reported
conflicting results for peak adduction moments in partici-
pants with ACLR, varying from low to high magnitude [17,
18]. In the sagittal plane, lower external flexion moments
were found following ACLR at mid-stance of walking at
2–12 months post-operatively compared with controls [19],
while no significant differences were reported on average
17 months post-surgery [20]. Decreased flexion moments
while walking and during stair navigation have also been
found in patients with knee OA. Furthermore, a recent
systematic review found increased flexion moments during
walking in patients with knee OA following joint
replacements, compared with pre-operative measures [21].
Flexion moments require an internal quadriceps moment to
counteract the forces of body weight [22]. Decreased
flexion moments are likely to indicate unloading of the
knee joint or a compensatory strategy, possibly due to
decreased neuromuscular control, lingering symptoms, and
hesitancy for weight-bearing on that side [23].
While several studies have explored gait biomechanics
following ACLR, various methodologies and tasks have
been used. Summarizing these gait biomechanics will
increase the understanding of possible impairments and
guide rehabilitation interventions to improve outcome and
decrease long-term disability. Previous reviews on recov-
ery of gait biomechanics following ACLR have either not
included meta-analysis [24] or analyzed only sagittal plane
moments [25]. Hart et al. [13] recently reviewed gait
analysis only during walking activity, finding deficits in
sagittal plane moments but not in the frontal plane. The
current review includes other activities of daily living,
namely stair ascent, descent, and running, in addition to
walking. It is possible that long-term impairments and
asymmetries following ACLR may be more evident during
those cyclical and repetitive activities that are associated
with higher joint loading than walking [26]. Thus, the
primary aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis
1870 M. Kaur et al.
123

--- PAGE 3 ---
was to compare knee kinematics and kinetics in individuals
with ACLR with the contralateral limb and with healthy
age-matched controls during three different tasks (walking,
stair ascent/descent, and running). The secondary aim was
to describe the progression over time of those biome-
chanical variables following ACLR.
2 Methods
2.1 Search Strategy and Study Selection
Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and
Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines were followed as
appropriate for observational studies [27]. Embase, MED-
LINE, Web of Science, and Scopus databases were sear-
ched from their original available dates to 1 July 2014, with
an update on 10 August 2015. Keywords used and the
search strategy are presented in Table 1.
The following inclusion criteria were applied: (1)
observational study designs (prospective cohort studies,
case-control studies, and cross-sectional studies) or ran-
domized clinical trials (RCTs) with the comparison with
control group or comparison with the contralateral unin-
jured side at baseline; (2) men and women, with isolated
ACL ruptures or in addition to menisci and other liga-
mentous injury of the knee, managed with reconstructions
with any type of graft; (3) studies estimating kinematic and
kinetic data (discrete variables: peak angles in the three
planes of movement, peak external knee flexion, and
adduction moments) of the ACLR knee and the asymp-
tomatic controls during walking, stair negotiation, or run-
ning. Studies focusing on other lower limb injuries, or
other tasks, such as jumping or pivoting, were excluded.
No language restrictions were applied. Two reviewers (MK
and GS) screened all relevant titles and abstracts and were
blinded to authors and journals. Full-text articles were
screened according to the pre-set inclusion and exclusion
criteria by the two reviewers. Any discrepancies were
resolved through consensus, and a third reviewer was
available if needed (DR). A manual search of the reference
lists of the included articles was also conducted.
2.2 Risk of Bias Within Included Studies
A modified version of the Downs and Black Quality Index
[28]wasusedtoassesstheriskofbiaswithinincludedstudies.
The modified checklist included 16 questions from the fol-
lowing sub-groups: reporting (items 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, and 10),
externalvalidity(items11and12),internalvaliditybias(item
15, 16, 18, and 20), internal validity confounding (selection
bias) (items 21 and 25), and power (item 27) (Electronic
Supplementary Material [ESM] Table S1). Item 25 relates to
confounding factors: walking or running speed were consid-
eredasthemostrelevantconfounders,asthesevariableshave
beenshowntobecorrelatedwithexternalkneeadductionand
flexion moments [29]. Thus, a score of ‘‘1’’ was applied if
speed of ambulation was not significantly different between
participant groups, or if appropriate statistical analyses were
performed, including speed as a covariate. Item 27 was
reworded as ‘‘Were appropriate power calculations repor-
ted?’’andthescorewaschangedfrom0–5toascaleof0or1.
Thestudy wasassigneda score of‘‘1’’ ifprior power analysis
was performed, with no scores being assigned in the absence
ofpoweranalysis.Theriskofbiasassessmentwas performed
independently by two reviewers (MK and GS), with discrep-
ancies resolved during consensus meetings. Kappa’s corre-
lation coefficient was calculated to determine the agreement
of the scores of the individual questions for each study
between the two reviewers. The modified Downs and Black
Quality Index was scored out of 17. Studies with scores of 11
and above (65 %) were considered to have a low risk of bias,
and studies with scores below 11 were considered to have a
high risk of bias [30].
2.3 Data Extraction and Meta-Analysis
Data extracted from each study included sample size,
participants’ demographics, type of functional activities,
and discrete variables for knee kinematics and kinetics
(i.e., peak angles and moments during the stance phase of
gait). For external adduction moments, the first of the two
peaks was extracted. Peak knee tibial rotations were
reported during the stance phase of gait. We contacted the
corresponding authors when relevant data were not pre-
sented or were published as graphs.

--- PAGE 4 ---
We used Review Manager v5.3 (RevMan) (Copen-
hagen: The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Col-
laboration, 2014) to perform the meta-analysis when more
than one study investigated the same dependent variable
during a given task using three-dimensional movement
analysis. The main aim of the forest plot was to determine
(standardized) mean differences and confidence intervals.
Effect sizes (ESs) and 95 % confidence intervals (CIs)
were calculated for between-group (ACLR groups vs.
uninjured control groups) and within-group (injured sides
vs. contralateral uninjured sides of the ACLR groups)
comparisons of kinematic data and kinetic data. Calculated
individual or pooled ESs were categorised as small (\0.5),
medium (C0.5 and\0.8), or large (C0.8) [31]. The level of
statistical heterogeneity for pooled data was established
using c2
and I2
statistics (heterogeneity defined as
p\0.05). For peak joint angles, we also calculated mean
differences (MDs) (net difference in peak angle among any
two groups) in degrees for findings of individual studies or
pooled data from two or more studies, as these may be
more easily translated to clinical practice than ESs.
To conduct between- and within-group comparisons of
the biomechanical variables over time, the included studies
were ordered in the forest plots according to ‘‘time since
surgery’’ (in weeks or months). The shortest time since
surgery was presented at the top, and the longest average
time since surgery was presented at the bottom of the forest
plot. This approach allowed a qualitative analysis of dif-
ferences in biomechanical variables between and within
groups over time.
2.4 Level of Evidence
ThelevelofevidencewasdefinedforeachvariableasperVan
Tulder et al. [32] as follows. (1) Strong evidence provided by
pooledresults derivedfromthree ormore studies,includinga
minimum of two studies with a low risk of bias, that are
homogenous(p[0.05);theanalysismaybeassociatedwitha
statistically significant or non-significant pooled results. (2)
Moderateevidenceprovidedbystatisticallysignificantpooled
results derived from multiple studies, including at least one
studywithlowriskofbias,thatarestatisticallyheterogeneous
(p\0.05), or from multiple studies with a high risk of bias
that are statistically homogenous (p[0.05). (3) Limited
evidenceprovidedbyresultsfrommultiplestudieswithahigh
risk of bias that are statistically heterogeneous (p\0.05), or
from one study with a low risk of bias. (4) Very limited evi-
dence provided by results from one study with a high risk of
bias. (5) Conflicting evidence provided by pooled results that
are insignificant and derived from multiple studies regardless
of quality that are statistically heterogeneous (p\0.05, i.e.,
inconsistent).
3 Results
3.1 Search Results
The first search yielded 1550 articles (Fig. 1); 65 remained
after excluding duplicates and irrelevant titles and screen-
ing abstracts. A further 25 studies were excluded based on
the inclusion and exclusion criteria, giving a final yield of
40 studies that were included in the qualitative analysis. Of
the studies, 37 were in English, two in German [33, 34],
and one in Chinese [35]. Data from 27 studies could be
included in meta-analyses.
3.2 Risk of Bias
Kappa’s correlation coefficient was 0.93 for the agreement
between the two reviewers for risk of bias assessment. Of
the 40 studies, 26 were rated as low risk and 14 as high risk
(Table 2). Seven corresponding authors were contacted to
request data for dependent variables [36–42]; one provided
the details [38]. Variables were calculated from the fig-
ures when corresponding authors did not respond [43–45].
3.3 Overview of Included Studies
A total of 31 studies included comparisons with asymp-
tomatic age-matched subjects, and nine with the con-
tralateral knee of this ACLR participant group (Table 3).
Kinematic and kinetic variables were studied during
walking in 37 studies at self-selected comfortable speed,
during stair ascent and descent in eight studies [42, 43, 46–
51], and during running in five studies [41, 43, 52–54]. The
number of included participants ranged from eight with
ACLR and ten controls [41, 52] to 45 in both groups [51],
and time since surgery ranged from 2 weeks [48] to
18 years [47].
An RCT conducted by Hooper et al. [48] was included
and, for the purpose of this review, the baseline compar-
isons for the injured versus the contralateral uninjured
knees were considered for the meta-analysis. A longitudi-
nal cross-sectional study by Webster et al. [55] was
included, with the results being reported at 1 year and
3.3 years. Data from both of these time periods were
included for meta-analysis.
Grand means and standard deviations (SDs) were cal-
culated [56] where studies presented results for different
groups with ACLR. In one study [48], baseline results of
participants undergoing either closed or open kinetic
training were combined. Where studies compared out-
comes of different surgical procedures, specifically,
between hamstring and patella tendon grafts [57, 58], sin-
gle- and double-bundle grafts [59], and use of different
1872 M. Kaur et al.
123

--- PAGE 5 ---
portal techniques [60], the results of the ACLR groups
were combined and compared with those of the controls.
Lewek et al. [52] included two groups of participants based
on quadriceps strength: (1) ‘‘strong ACLR’’ group and (2)
‘‘weak ACLR’’ group. The data of these two groups were
combined into a grand mean and SD. Furthermore, vari-
ables for participants with ACLR for the dominant and
non-dominant limbs were combined and compared with the
control group in a study by Wang et al. [39]. Results of two
groups reported by Di Stasi et al. [61], participants who
passed ‘return to sports’ criteria and those who did not
pass, were also combined into grand means and SDs, cal-
culated from the published 95 % CIs. In another study by
Di Stasi et al. [45], means and CIs were estimated from the
given figure and grand mean and SDs for injured and
uninjured sides were calculated, combining the results for
men and women. Roewer et al. [44] conducted a longitu-
dinal study, reporting data at 6 months and at 2 years post-
reconstruction. CIs were estimated from the figure, and
SDs were calculated. Data reported at both time periods
were included in the forest plots [44].
3.4 Meta-Analyses
Meta-analyses were conducted for peak angles and
moments (peak knee flexion and adduction moments)
during the stance phase of gait (Figs. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7).
Tables 4 and 5 provide the ESs and CIs for the meta-
analyses and for variables that were explored in one study
only. Mean differences for joint angles are provided in
Table S2 in the ESM.
3.4.1 Joint Angles
Peak knee flexion angles during walking were reported in
11 studies [44, 47, 48, 50, 52, 54, 55, 57, 61–63]. The meta-
analysis indicated strong evidence for no difference com-
pared with controls [47, 52, 54, 57, 62, 63] and moderate
evidence for less flexion for the ACLR compared with the
contralateral limb (ES -0.06; 95 % CI -0.8 to -0.4; MD
4.3°) [44, 47, 48, 55, 61]. A sensitivity test was performed
by excluding a study by Hooper et al. [48], as this study
compared ACLR participants at 2 weeks post-

there was moderate evidence that peak flexion was
decreased for ACLR knees compared with controls during
stair descent (Fig. 2 [2.1.5]). During running, no significant
differences were found for the knee flexion angle compared
with controls (Fig. 2 [2.1.6]).
Only three studies reported peak knee adduction angles
(Fig. 3), with a range from 7.5 months to 5.3 years post-
reconstruction [17, 40, 63]. The meta-analysis indicated
moderate evidence for no significant difference between
the ACLR knee and controls.
In terms of rotation at the knee, studies either reported
maximal external or internal tibial rotation during the
loading phase [53, 58–60, 63]. Strong evidence indicated
no significant difference for external tibial rotation for
ACLR knees compared with controls during walking
(maximum 17 months post-surgery, Fig. 4). While peak
external rotation angles were considered for analysis,
Czamara et al. [59] reported external rotation at initial
foot contact. Their results were included into the meta-
analysis, as peak external rotation is most likely to occur
at heel strike phase during the stance phase of the
walking gait [64]. One study [50] found less external
rotation for the ACLR knees at 3 months post-surgery
during stair descent (ES -1.1; 95 % CI -2 to -0.2; MD
-5.8°; 95 % CI -1.8 to -9.9). Strong evidence was
found for less tibial internal rotation (ES -0.7; 95 % CI
-1.1 to -0.4) (Fig. 5) for ACLR knees compared with
the contralateral limbs during walking [53, 55, 58].
However, results of one study [41] indicated no signifi-
cant difference between the ACLR and the contralateral
limbs while running, with limited evidence (ES -1.1;
95 % CI -2.3 to 0).
3.4.2 Joint Moments
Overall, participants with ACLR presented with signifi-
cantly lower peak flexion moments during walking than
controls and the contralateral limbs (strong evidence)
(Fig. 6 [6.2.1, 6.2.2]). Strong evidence was found for peak
flexion moments being lower for the injured side than for
the contralateral uninjured sides during walking, stair
ascent, and descent after ACLR (Fig. 6 [6.2.3–6.2.6]).
Moderate evidence indicated no significant differences
during running in ACLR participants compared with con-
trols (Fig. 6 [6.2.7]).
The meta-analysis showed moderate to strong evidence
for significantly lower first peak adduction moments during
walking for the ACLR knees when compared with controls
and with the contralateral limbs, respectively (Fig. 7 [7.1.1,
7.1.2]). Strong and moderate evidence indicated no sig-
nificant differences were present for the peak adduction
moments during stair ascent and descent, respectively, for
the ACLR knees compared with the control group (Fig. 7
Fig. 4 Forest plot for peak tibial external rotation angle during stance phase of gait during walking compared with control group. ACLR anterior

--- PAGE 20 ---
[7.1.3, 7.1.5]). In contrast, lower peak adduction moments
were found for ACLR during stair ascent (moderate evi-
dence) and descent (strong evidence) compared with the
contralateral limbs (Fig. 7 [7.1.4, 7.1.6]). No studies eval-
uating adduction moments during running were identified
and included in the review.
ES for differences for the flexion and adduction
moments were low (\0.59) for all comparisons, except for
the comparison of flexion moments during stair ascent (ES
0.7, 95 % CI 0.1 to 0.4) and descent (ES 0.5, 95 % CI 0.1
to 0.8) when comparing ACLR knees with the contralateral
limbs.
3.5 Time Course of Recovery
The qualitative assessment of the forest plots suggests
patients tend to restore peak knee flexion angle over time
after surgery for studies that included participants up to
6 years, and present peak knee flexion angle that is similar
to the contralateral limb (Fig. 2). However, such an
Fig. 7 Forest plot for first peak of knee adduction moment during stance phase of gait in different activities. ACLR anterior cruciate ligament
reconstruction, CI confidence interval, IV inverse variance, SD standard deviation
1888 M. Kaur et al.
123

--- PAGE 21 ---
improvement over time was not evident for peak flexion
moments during walking. When ascending and descending
stairs, patients tended to present improved flexion moments
over time when compared with the contralateral sides, but
not when compared with controls (Fig. 6).
During walking, peak adduction moments appeared to
be significantly lower in participants with ACLR than in
controls within the first year following surgery (average
9.4 months) [70]. However, while not significant (95 % CI
-0.02 to 1.4), these adduction moments showed a tendency
to be slightly higher than in controls at a later phase
(5.3 years) [40] (Fig. 7). Interestingly, Karimi et al. [65]
found higher peak adduction moments at 6 months post-
reconstruction than for controls. Functional braces were
worn by their participants for 3 months post-surgery; none
of the other studies reported these being worn. A sensitivity
test was performed by excluding the adduction moments
for this study [65], and the results indicate that, overall,
peak adduction moments were significantly lower in the
ACLR group than in the control group (ES -0.32, 95 % CI
-0.55 to -0.08). When excluding their results, there
appears to be a response in time, from lower to equivalent
adduction moments for the ACLR group compared with
controls while walking.
4 Discussion
The primary aim of this review was to investigate knee
joint angles and moments in participants with ACLR
compared with the contralateral limbs and with age-
matched controls during walking, stair climbing, and
running. In terms of joint angles, moderate to strong
evidence was found for no differences for peak flexion
during walking, stair ascent, and jogging when compar-
ing the ACLR knees with controls. However, when
compared with the uninjured contralateral sides, less
flexion and less internal rotation was found for the ACLR
knees during walking. During stair descent, peak flexion
was decreased for ACLR knees compared with controls.
There was moderate evidence for no differences for peak
adduction angles between the ACLR knee and controls.
Moderate to strong evidence was found for lower peak
flexion moments in participants with ACLR during
walking and stair ascent compared with controls and with
the contralateral limbs. Moderate to strong evidence also
indicated lower peak adduction moment for the ACLR
knees during walking and stair ascent and descent than
for the contralateral limbs, and during walking compared
with the controls.

4.1 Peak Joint Angles
Results of the meta-analysis suggest that participants with
ACLR regain similar peak knee flexion angles compared
with the control group during walking by 6 years following
surgery (Fig. 2). However, pooled peak flexion angles were
lower in the ACLR knee than in the contralateral sides (ES
0.6;95 %CI-0.4to-0.8).TheMDof4.3°washigherthan
theminimalclinicallyimportantdifferenceof3°reportedfor
knee flexion during the stance phase of walking [66]. This
difference was influenced in part by the findings by Hooper
et al. [48] at 2 weeks post-surgery: the MD was 8.5°, which
may be due to pain or swelling at early stages after surgery.
Consideringtheindividualstudies,limbasymmetryforpeak
flexion angles was evident until 6 months post-reconstruc-
tion [44, 61], while no significant bilateral differences were
found, on average, 10 months to 6 years following surgery.
Similarly, our meta-analysis indicated no significant
between-group differences for knee adduction and external
rotation angles during walking. However, peak external
rotation was decreased during stair descent based on one
study [50]. Internal rotation was decreased during walking
for the ACLR knee compared with the contralateral limb.
Rotational shifts varied from 1 to 5.8°. A biomechanical
model of degeneration showed that a 5° rotational shift
may be enough to cause accelerated degeneration of the
cartilage [67] due to alterations in the stresses applied to
joint surfaces [68]. Whether these small differences in
kinematics for participants with ACLR compared with
controls and contralateral limbs indicate an increased risk
for PTOA still needs confirmation.
4.2 Joint Moments
Strong evidence was found that peak flexion moments were
significantly lower in participants with ACLR during
walking and stair ascent and descent activities compared
with controls and contralateral limbs. However, the ESs

were small during walking and when compared with the
controls during stair ascent and descent, while moderate
ESs were found for decreased flexion moments when
compared with the contralateral sides during stair ascent
and descent. It is thus possible that an asymmetry may be
more evident during stair ascent and descent than during
walking. Peak external flexion moments are considered to
reflect net quadriceps function [69], and reduced moments
may be associated with lower quadriceps strength [22].
Neurophysiological changes following ACL injury and
reconstruction have been shown to include decreased lower
limb muscle activation, as determined by electromyogra-
phy in ACLR knees [70] and lower cortical activation in
injured limbs compared with an uninjured and healthy
population, contributing towards reduced net quadriceps
function [71]. The presence of pain, reported even at
2–5 years after surgery [72], or reflex inhibition [73], could
further influence the movement patterns, as apparent with
reduced flexion moments. Furthermore, compensatory
movements at the hip and trunk may also decrease knee
joint loading [74]. It is thus likely that multiple mecha-
nisms contribute towards long-term decreased flexion
moments in the ACLR knees.
Similar to external knee flexion moments, the adduction
moments for the ACLR knees were significantly smaller
during walking than for controls, albeit with low ESs. No
significant differences were found for either the flexion
moments or the adduction moments during stair descent for
the ACLR knees compared with the controls, while they
were lower for the ACLR knees than for the contralateral
side. This indicates a bilateral asymmetry during this task
and could infer that, during stair descent, the contralateral
side has higher flexion and adduction moments than con-
trols. While this is speculative, compensatory patterns may
be evident for the contralateral side [25], which are likely
due to central nervous system changes following the injury
and surgery. Such changes have been documented in
patients with ACL-deficient knees [74].
The meta-analysis along with sensitivity test for one
study [65] showed peak adduction moments were lower in
ACLR participants than in controls in the short and med-
ium term (up to 3.5 years) and higher as time following
reconstruction progresses. Our findings contrast thus with
those by Hart et al. [13], who recently found that the frontal
plane moments may not be affected by ACLR. Thus, our
findings suggest that frontal plane moments cannot yet be
disregarded as outcomes and long-term consequences of
ACLR. The finding of lower adduction moments in the
ACLR knees contrast with increased adduction moments
often reported in patients with knee OA [83]. Risk of
progression of OA in patients with that disorder increases
6.46 times with a 1 % increase in adduction moments [15],
hence the magnitude of adduction moments is correlated
with OA severity [12, 16]. While decreased adduction
moments in the early phase following ACLR may reflect
decreased weight-bearing and compensatory strategies of
the trunk, hip, and ankle [83–85], a combination of
changing flexion and adduction moments and joint rota-
tions may contribute towards loading at unconditioned
areas of the cartilage, potentially leading to development of
OA [75]. Studies included in the present review did not
report radiographic OA changes for their participants;
therefore, whether those with higher adduction moments
present with radiographic signs of OA is unknown [15].
Whether changes for external adduction moments during
functional tasks predict onset of OA following ACLR still
needs to be substantiated. While the development of OA is
multi-factorial, these biomechanical factors should be
explored longitudinally in all planes.
4.3 Clinical Implications
Overall, reduced flexion and adduction moments indicate
altered joint loading in the long term following ACLR.
These changes are likely associated with quadriceps
weakness [76] and various neurophysiological mechanisms
[77–79], and are potentially associated with risk of early-
onset joint degeneration [80, 81] due to suboptimal joint
loading during functional tasks such as walking, running,
and stair navigation [82]. Altered kinematics, along with
reduced flexion moments, may significantly change the
stress distribution within the cartilage and initiate a
degenerative process [83]. Di Stasi et al. [61] showed that
athletes with superior functional performance at 6 months
following ACLR appear to demonstrate less asymmetrical
gait patterns than those that did not pass functional ‘return
to play’ criteria. Therefore, it appears to be important to
include assessment of potential gait asymmetries following
ACLR in decision making for readiness for rehabilitation
progression and return to sports [61, 84]. While small
differences in walking may not be detectable on clinical
examination, these may be more evident during high knee-
loading activities, such as stair ascent/descent, running
[84], and jumping [85]. The finding of movement and
loading asymmetries in the current review indicate that it
may be important for people with ACRL to continue with
exercise programs focusing on strength, neuromuscular
control, and proprioception even after the rehabilitation
period is completed.
4.4 Methodological Considerations and Directions
for Future Research
The risk-of-bias assessment identified methodological
limitations for the included studies: the absence of outcome
measurer blinding, reporting reliability of methodology,
Movement Patterns of the Knee after ACL Reconstruction 1891
123

--- PAGE 24 ---
lack of confounding factors such as control of gait speed,
and a priori power calculation for sample size. While
blinding of the researcher is difficult during data collection
due to visible scarring at the operated knee, blinding for the
participant group (control vs. ACLR) can be maintained
while processing kinematic and kinetic data.
A total of 16 studies included in the meta-analysis
controlled the speed of the tasks [17, 19, 38, 40, 41, 43–45,
52, 54, 57, 60–63, 86]. A compensatory strategy to main-
tain or decrease joint loading is to walk slower [87]. Thus,
in those studies where speed was not reported, it is possible
that participants with ACLR may have walked slower,
thereby maintaining or controlling the joint loading effec-
tively. This could lead to no significant differences between
groups, as seen for stair descent for flexion and adduction
moments. Furthermore, other compensatory strategies that
develop over time post-reconstruction, such as transferring
the load to the hip and ankle [88] and compensation with
trunk lean, can also be used to decrease joint moments, as
shown in patients with knee OA [89, 90]. These factors
should be addressed in future research.
Only cross-sectional studies or baseline measures of
RCTs were considered for the purpose of time course of
recovery analysis in this review. However, longitudinal
studies following patients at different time points following
ACLR are needed to fully investigate how gait biome-
chanics change over time, and how these changes may
influence the development of OA or re-injury. Furthermore,
the aim of this review was to explore differences for peak
knee joint angles and moments when comparing people
with ACLR versus controls, and not between different
surgical or rehabilitative programs. Findings of groups of
participants with ACLR undergoing different procedures
within individual studies were thus combined into grand
means for the meta-analyses, which masks differences
between these groups. Findings of this review are thus
limited to comparisons with controls and when comparing
the ACLR knees to the contralateral uninjured sides, irre-
spective of surgical methods. Finally, this review was
limited to the discrete variables of peak angles and
moments, and did not explore biomechanical variables in
other phases of the gait cycle.
5 Conclusion
Joint kinematics of ACLR knees were found to be similar
to control groups during walking and stair navigation
within a few months after surgery. However, differences in
knee external moments persist over a longer period. The
meta-analysis indicated lower pooled external flexion
moments for people with ACLR than for controls during
walking and stair ascent. The meta-analysis also indicated
decreased peak adduction moments during walking and
stair navigation for ACLR knees, specifically when com-
pared with contralateral limbs. Based on individual studies
included in the review, such moments may be lower than
for controls in the early phase following ACLR
(10 months), but higher at a later phase (5 years) after
surgery. While this review did not explore compensatory
mechanisms, it is likely that multiple mechanisms influ-
ence altered gait patterns, including changes in muscle
function and neuromuscular control at the trunk, hip, knee,
and ankle. Gait patterns at the knee are not fully restored
after more than 5 years following surgery. This finding
indicates that long-term rehabilitative or maintenance
programs may need to be considered for patients under-
going ACLR.

review. Gisela Sole was responsible for the conception of this review;
Mandeep Kaur conducted the entire review, with Gisela Sole and
Daniel Cury Ribeiro as second and third reviewers; Jean-Claude Theis
and Kate Webster provided advice throughout the review. All authors
were involved with the final manuscript.
